Survey-intensity surface (the S term) as a continuous Gaussian field

Source: R/fn_survey.R
survey.Rd

Builds the manuscript's survey intensity term S — the “bias surface” — from target-group occurrence records (a GBIF pull of co-occurring taxa), as a continuous field of the landscape rather than a grid. The estimator is a weighted sum of isotropic Gaussian kernels, one per record:

Details

$$S(x) \;=\; \sum_{j}\, w_j \sum_{i \in j} \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\lVert x - p_{ij} \rVert^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big),$$

where \(p_{ij}\) is record \(i\) of species \(j\), \(\sigma\) is the single search-radius bandwidth, and \(w_j\) is a per-species weight.

Why it is built this way

  • Gridless / resolution-free. \(S(x)\) is a closed-form function of position, defined everywhere. Points are never binned to a grid before modelling; the model is the kernel sum. A raster is only ever a downstream view of the field, rendered at whatever resolution the user asks for (survey_raster), and two resolutions are two views of one model.

  • Additive across species. The outer sum is over species, so each taxon contributes an independent layer \(w_j K_j(x)\). A species can be added or dropped by adding/subtracting its term; eval_survey can be restricted to a subset of species to recover any single layer.

  • Inverse-frequency weighting, domain-corrected (see survey_weights). Common taxa are uninformative about effort (they are everywhere); a record of a seldom-collected taxon marks a careful search. Let \(n_j\) be the record count and \(\varphi_j\) the proportion of the species' p95 bounding box that falls inside the domain. The effective in-domain frequency is \(f_j = n_j / \varphi_j\) and \(w_j = (\varphi_j / n_j)^{\mathrm{damp}}\). The \(\varphi_j\) correction stops a species whose range merely clips the domain edge from looking spuriously rare (and so over-weighted). Because \(\varphi_j \le 1 \le n_j\), the raw weight \(w_j \in (0, 1]\) needs no cap: a fully-in-domain singleton earns the maximum weight 1, a common or edge-clipping taxon decays toward 0.

Direction into the index. Well-surveyed ground is less likely to hide an undocumented population, so the RankIndex wants survey sparsity: render with invert = TRUE to get \(1 - \tilde S\), high where nobody has looked.

terra for the raster view and sf for the p95-box/domain overlap. The kernel is truncated at trunc\(\,\sigma\) (tails below \(e^{-8}\) at trunc = 4) and evaluated with a tiled bounding-box prefilter, so no kd-tree dependency and no \(k\)-neighbour cap — the sum is exact to the tail.
